curriculum.title: New Covenant and Renewed Creation Promises

core.big_idea: The prophets anticipate forgiveness, transformed people, restored presence, and renewed creation.

passages.reading_note: Read the promise to the houses of Israel and Judah, noting covenant contrast, internal law, knowledge, and forgiveness.
Read cleansing, new heart, new spirit, God's Spirit, obedience, land, and belonging in context.
Read as prophetic new-creation poetry, noting joy, life, work, peace, and imagery.
Examine the New Testaments quotation and application of Jeremiah 31.
Use for older teens to compare written-on-heart and Spirit language.
Use to trace renewed creation and divine presence without forcing every prophetic image into a literal one-to-one chart.

core.metanarrative_position: Exilic and post-exilic prophetic hope: God promises covenant renewal, forgiveness, inner transformation, restored presence, and creation renewal, which the New Testament applies to Christ, the Spirit, the church, and final hope.
core.biblical_genre: Prophetic promise, restoration oracle, covenant quotation, and apocalyptic vision

claims.statement: Jeremiah promises a new covenant with Israel and Judah that differs from the covenant broken after the Exodus.
Jeremiah describes internalised law, direct covenant knowledge, and decisive forgiveness.
Ezekiel promises cleansing, a new heart and spirit, God's Spirit, renewed obedience, land, and restored belonging for God's names sake.
Isaiah 65 uses new-heavens-and-new-earth imagery to portray joy, security, fruitful work, long life, and peace.
Hebrews applies Jeremiah 31 to the superior covenant mediated by Jesus.
Christian canonical synthesis connects prophetic covenant and creation promises to present life in Christ and the Spirit while also retaining future consummation hope.
Interpreters disagree about the timing, recipients, literal or symbolic dimensions, and Israel-church relationship within these promises.
claims.credible_alternative: Dispensational, covenantal, restorationist, Jewish, and other readings differ on national Israel, church participation, land, fulfilment timing, and renewed-creation imagery.
claims.interpretive_hinge: How original audiences, New Testament quotation, inaugurated fulfilment, future hope, land language, and prophetic imagery relate.
claims.prohibited_overstatement: Do not erase Israel and Judah from the original promise, claim every image is already fully realised, or force one millennial system as a salvation test.

core.interpretation_skill: Read prophetic imagery in original exile context, trace explicit New Testament appropriation, and distinguish inaugurated claims, future hope, and disputed fulfilment models.

learning.foundation_objective: Analyse Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Isaiah and explain the connected hopes of forgiveness, transformation, restored presence, and renewed creation.
learning.extension_objective: Evaluate New Testament appropriation while distinguishing original audience, present covenant participation, future consummation, prophetic imagery, and disputed Israel-church models.
know: Ezekiel links cleansing, new heart, Spirit, obedience, land, and belonging.
Hebrews quotes Jeremiah and applies it to Jesus covenant mediation.
understand: Prophetic hope is moral, relational, communal, and cosmic rather than merely private escape.
Fulfilment can involve present participation and future completion without flattening every image.
practise: Pray for genuine inward transformation rather than religious appearance.
Act as a sign of forgiveness, peace, faithful work, or care for creation.
become: A student who hopes biblically, reads prophetic imagery carefully, and resists both escapism and overconfident timetables.
success_evidence: The student compares the three prophetic passages.
The student identifies Hebrews explicit use of Jeremiah.
The student states one disputed hinge without caricature.
The student proposes one present practice consistent with future hope.

zero_prep_card.objective: Students explain how prophetic promises connect forgiveness, inner renewal, God's presence, and renewed creation.
zero_prep_card.opening: Ask: What would genuine restoration require beyond rebuilding a city or changing external rules?
say: Jeremiah promises a new covenant to Israel and Judah after covenant failure.
Ezekiel adds cleansing, a new heart, God's Spirit, obedience, land, and restored belonging.
Isaiah widens hope through poetic new-creation imagery of joy, work, life, and peace.
Hebrews explicitly applies Jeremiah's covenant promise to Jesus superior covenant, while interpreters still debate timing and the relation of Israel, church, and future fulfilment.
ask: What does Hebrews explicitly claim and what remains debated?
zero_prep_card.do: Complete the Prophetic Hope Matrix: Problem, Promise, Original Audience, New Testament Use, Future Question.
zero_prep_card.close: Pray for forgiveness, transformed hearts, the Spirits work, faithful present living, and the completion of God's renewal.

preparation.passage_context: Jeremiah and Ezekiel speak amid covenant breakdown and exile. Isaiah 65 presents restoration through expansive poetic imagery. Hebrews quotes Jeremiah directly and argues for a better covenant mediated by Jesus. Revelation later reuses new-creation and divine-presence imagery.
text_observations: Jeremiah names the houses of Israel and Judah and compares the new covenant with the broken Exodus covenant.
Knowledge and forgiveness in Jeremiah are covenant-wide, not merely private feelings.
Ezekiel says the action protects God's holy name and combines cleansing, heart, Spirit, obedience, land, and belonging.
Isaiah 65 contains features that complicate a simplistic literal final-state reading, including death and long life within new-creation imagery.
Hebrews 8 quotes Jeremiah and draws a covenantal conclusion, but does not answer every later system question.
interpretation_notes: Keep original audience visible before Christian appropriation.
Distinguish metaphor, poetic idealisation, typology, and direct doctrinal statement.
Avoid reducing new covenant to private forgiveness only; the passages include transformed community and divine presence.
Avoid reducing new creation to disembodied escape; the imagery values life, work, peace, and God's dwelling.
theological_guardrails: Do not erase Israel and Judah from the original covenant promise or use replacement language carelessly.
Do not force premillennial, amillennial, or postmillennial timing as a fellowship or salvation test.
Do not claim complete present sinlessness or that every covenant member automatically lives without struggle.
Do not use new heart language to dismiss mental health, trauma, disability, or the need for practical care.
Do not describe renewed creation in more physical or nonphysical detail than the texts support.

likely_questions.question: Is the new covenant already fulfilled?
likely_questions.purpose: Hebrews says Jesus mediates the better covenant and applies Jeremiah to its readers. Christians disagree about what is inaugurated now, what remains future, and how Israel and church relate.

likely_questions.question: Will the new creation be physical or spiritual?
likely_questions.purpose: The approved curriculum teaches resurrection, return, judgment, and new spiritual creation without forcing one millennial system. Biblical texts use embodied, cosmic, relational, and symbolic language; avoid certainty beyond the evidence.

likely_questions.question: Does everyone in the new covenant know God perfectly?
likely_questions.purpose: Jeremiah gives an ideal covenant promise. Hebrews applies it covenantally, while lived experience and fulfilment timing raise interpretive questions. Do not use the verse to claim complete present knowledge or sinlessness.

discussion_questions.question: What makes the covenant new in Jeremiah 31?
discussion_questions.foundation_prompt: Internal law, covenant knowledge, forgiveness, and contrast with the broken covenant.
discussion_questions.extension_prompt: Explain both continuity and discontinuity without importing a whole system prematurely.

discussion_questions.question: What does Ezekiel's sequence reveal about restoration?
discussion_questions.foundation_prompt: Cleansing, new heart, Spirit, obedience, land, and belonging.
discussion_questions.extension_prompt: Analyse divine initiative, purpose for God's name, and human transformation.

discussion_questions.question: How should Isaiah 65s imagery be read?
discussion_questions.foundation_prompt: As prophetic new-creation poetry using concrete restoration images.
discussion_questions.extension_prompt: Explain why death and long life complicate a flat literal map of the final state.

discussion_questions.question: What does Hebrews settle and what remains disputed?
discussion_questions.foundation_prompt: It applies Jeremiah to Jesus better covenant.
discussion_questions.extension_prompt: Identify unresolved questions about timing, Israel, church, land, and consummation.

activities.title: Prophetic Hope Matrix
steps: Record each passages original audience and crisis.
activities.learning_link: Prevents proof-texting and flattening of distinct prophetic texts.
activities.low_resource_alternative: Build the matrix on a board.

activities.title: Already, Not Yet, or Disputed?
steps: Classify complete end of death and sorrow.
Classify land and national restoration claims.
Defend each classification with evidence and uncertainty labels.
activities.learning_link: Practises calibrated eschatological reasoning without imposing one system.

closing.prayer_prompt: Pray for forgiveness, inward renewal, Spirit-enabled faithfulness, and the completion of God's promised restoration.
closing.take_home_line: Prophetic hope joins forgiveness, transformed people, God's presence, and renewed creation.

family.title: A Bigger Picture of Restoration
family.parent_intro: This study compares three prophetic promises and the New Testaments explicit use of Jeremiah.

flow.instructions: Use the opening prompt to connect the lesson to ordinary family life.
Read Jeremiah 31:31-34, Ezekiel 36:25-28, and Hebrews 8:6-13. Summarise Isaiah 65:17-25.
List what God forgives, changes, gives, restores, and renews.
Sort claim cards into explicit prophecy, New Testament use, present application, future hope, or disputed model.
Choose the weekly action, then pray together.

questions: What restoration is communal or cosmic?

interactive.title: Restoration Claim Sort
interactive.instructions: Classify five claims and identify the evidence for each.

family.weekly_action: Choose one practice that anticipates renewal: forgive, make peace, care for creation, or do faithful work.
family.prayer: God, forgive us, renew our hearts, give Your Spirit, and bring Your promised creation to completion.
family.parent_note: Do not force agreement on one end-times system. Keep Israel and Judah visible in the original promise and avoid speculative detail.

accessibility.reading_level: Teen discussion with technical terms defined and claims tested against context.
accessibility.plain_language_rule: Use precise language; define specialist terms and separate evidence from conclusion.
neurodiversity_supports: Allow written rather than spoken responses.
sensory_notes: No required role-play, public disclosure, or competitive performance.
non_reader_support: Provide concise claim cards or summaries without replacing the biblical text.

do_not_ask: Do not test a students salvation by agreement with one fulfilment model.
Do not use new heart language to blame mental illness, trauma, or disability.
Do not invite partisan debate over modern territorial claims.
Do not use fear-based end-times speculation.
safeguarding.teacher_response: Keep disagreement evidence-based and non-coercive. Redirect personal distress or fear to a trusted adult and appropriate pastoral support.
